list.listitem: Suspect osteosarcoma in a patient with bone pain and swelling, especially in children and patients with a history of retinoblastoma, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, or Paget's Disease. B
When osteosarcoma is suspected, obtain radiographs with at least 2 views, followed by MRI and biopsy if abnormal or symptoms persist. B
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with limb-salvage surgery is the treatment of choice. B
Metastasis, which is the leading cause of death, most commonly spread to the lung. C
Close surveillance of patients following treatment should include history, physical examination, and radiographs of the chest and primary tumor site at regular intervals. B

background.definition: A cancer of the bone that usually affects the large bones of the arm or leg. It occurs most commonly in young people and affects more males than females. Also called osteogenic sarcoma.

list.listitem: 4.8 per 1,000,000 (per year) in children less than 20 years old. Incidence varies by ethnicity and gender: 5.2 per million per year in blacks, 4.6 per million per year in whites; 5.2 per million per year in males, 4.5 per million per year in females.

Age-adjusted incidence rates:
Age 0 to 4 years: 0.5 per million per year Age 5 to 9 years: 2.6 (black) or 2.1 (white) cases per million per year Age 10 to 14 years: 8.3 (black) or 7 (white) cases per million per year Age 15 to 19 years: 8.9 (black) or 8.2 (white) cases per million per year
Accounts for greater than 10% of all solid cancer in adolescents (ages 15-19 years) and is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents.
Etiology is unknown with most cases sporadic but several associations have been identified.
Mutations in retinoblastoma pathway; patients with retinoblastoma are more likely to have cancer later in life, 50% of which are osteosarcoma.
Mutations in p53 tumor suppressor gene pathway including Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
Ionizing radiation has been implicated in approximately 3% of osteosarcoma.
Exact pathophysiology remains unknown.

The working hypothesis is that a combination of germline mutations and/or exposure to radiation or chemotherapy along with rapid bone growth (usually during the adolescent growth spurt) predisposes individuals to the formation of malignant tumor at the metaphysis.
Suspect osteosarcoma in a patient with persistent bone pain, especially if accompanied by swelling. B
When osteosarcoma is suspected, obtain radiographs with at least 2 views. B
Order MRI if radiographs are abnormal or symptoms persist. B
Biopsy is the definitive mode of diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Other malignant tumors including Ewing sarcoma and chondrosarcoma
Benign tumors including osteoid osteoma, chondroblastoma, and osteochondroma
Differential.Differential_Features: X-ray appearance, No adjacent invasion or metastasis
X- ray appearance in characteristic location of tendon insertion, relief with rest

list.listitem: Staging by the Surgical Staging System, also known as the Enneking staging system, has been adopted as the staging system of the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society (see ).

Suspect osteosarcoma in any patient presenting with bony pain, particularly in the absence of injury. Pain is typically at the tumor location both at rest and at night. Pain can follow a sports injury, which may delay diagnosis. Patients may also have constitutional signs of fever and weight loss.

A palpable mass may or may not be seen. Because of increased vascularity, a bruit may be heard. There are usually limitations in range of motion once there is joint involvement. Lymphadenopathy is usually not present.

In a Swedish series of 102 patients with osteosarcoma, the following signs and symptoms were present at the time of diagnosis: local tenderness (92%), pain related to strain (85%), palpable mass (40%), painful movement of joint (40%), restricted movement of joint (23%), limp (28%), night pain (21%), atrophy of muscle (5%), and fever (3%). About half of patients associated the onset of pain to a minor injury, and delay in diagnosis because of misattribution of the pain to a strain or sprain was common.

20-30% of patients with malignant bone tumors present with metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis, with 5-year survival rates ranging from 8% to 35%, depending on the tumor’s histology. 85% to 90% of these metastases will be pulmonary.

Further research is needed at this time for possible biomarkers for osteosarcoma; however MMP9, SNVs in 9 genes, WNT6, as well as BCAR4 show promise for determining risk as well as progression of disease. For example, a case-control study found that WNT56 is 78% sensitive and 88% specific, with controls being patients with Ewing's sarcoma, osteomyelitis, or no disease.

Radiographs with at least 2 views, are the most appropriate initial test if an osteosarcoma is suspected. The classic X-ray finding is a "sunburst" appearance once the tumor has spread through the periosteum. Codman's triangle, a triangle-shaped area of irregular reactive bone growing from normal bone, is seen when periosteal lifting occurs at the metaphysis. Radiographs may also show cortical destruction.
MRI with gadolinium is recommended if symptoms persist despite negative X-ray or for staging if X-ray is suspicious for malignancy. CT scan is test of choice if there is a contraindication to MRI.

Staging is essential prior to treatment to evaluate for extent of local tumor involvement and for distant metastasis. An MRI of the local tumor site should be obtained to determine the extent of tumor involvement in the bone and surrounding soft tissues prior to treatment. It is useful to evaluate the location of surrounding anatomic structures as well as "skip" metastases.

A small study suggested that single photon emission CT (SPECT) was similarly sensitive and somewhat more specific than chest CT for localization of pulmonary metastases. A second small study found that CT was only 34% sensitive for detection of pulmonary nodules based on comparison with surgical findings.
CT of head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis with and without contrast and whole body nuclear bone scan are the tests of choice to look for metastasis in soft tissue and bone, respectively.

There is evidence that 2-(18F) fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG) PET may be useful in evaluating osteosarcoma, potential metastases, and recurrence; however, further studies are needed. The diagnostic sensitivities and specificities were 98% and 90% using FDG, and 81.6% and 80% using technetium-99m-MIBI SPECT, respectively.

FDG PET/CT shows significantly greater accuracy in detection of bone lesions on follow-up than CT alone and is complementary to CT in detection of lung lesions. TcMDP/HMDP scintigraphy is useful to assess the histological response of osteosarcoma to chemotherapy. FDG may not be readily available in many facilites.

Biopsy is the only way to make a definitive diagnosis; however, care must be taken during biopsy to preserve the bone for hopes of limb salvage. Histologic examination must include findings of immature bone tissue including osteoid. CT-guided needle biopsy remains the preferred technique for both adults and children.
Other tests include alkaline phosphatase and lactate dehydrogenase, which when elevated, are associated with a greater likelihood of adverse outcomes.
Consider an audiogram and echocardiogram prior to initiating chemotherapy.
Suspect osteosarcoma in patients with a persistently painful bone lesion, where a poorly marginated lesion is seen on a plain radiograph.
Order radiographs. If abnormal or if symptoms persist, consider MRI. Biopsy is required for diagnosis; however, complete staging should be performed prior to biopsy.
See algorithm in Figure 1 for a recommended approach to treatment.

Patients over the age of 40 years need a careful evaluation for a primary tumor including CXR, chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT, bone scan, mammogram, and other imaging studies, as clinically indicated.
Surgical excision with wide margins is the ultimate curative treatment of the primary tumor site. C
Some evidence to show that resection of metastases (in addition to the primary site) is not associated with improvement in overall survival, needs to be weighed against the risk of further surgeries.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended to evaluate the response of the tumor, to reduce the risk of systemic metastasis, and to aid with surgical excision. B
Limb-salvage surgical excision with wide margins is preferred to amputation with no difference in tumor recurrence. B

Multimodal therapy including chemotherapy and surgical excision improves survival from 10% to 50% to 60%. There is limited use for radiotherapy. It is used in patients who are refractory to chemotherapy.

Chemotherapy prior to surgery has not been shown to increase event-free survival when compared to chemotherapy following surgical excision. However, neoadjuvant, presurgical chemotherapy has been useful to determine whether the individual tumor is a good versus poor responder to treatment.

In extraskeletal osteosarcoma a meta-analysis comparing the two varieties of chemotherapy (platinum based treatment for osteosarcoma and doxorubicin/ifosfamide combination used in soft tissue sarcomas) given pre-operatively, demonstrated improved disease free survival at five years with the osteosarcoma regimens.

Doxorubicin, cisplatin, high-dose methotrexate with leucovorin rescue, and ifosfamide are currently considered the most active agents against osteosarcoma. However, RCTs comparing methotrexate against placebo are lacking. One small study showed equal efficacy with cisplatin.An Italian RCT of patients treated with methotrexate, cisplatin, and doxorubicin with or without ifosfamide in patients with non-metastatic extremity osteosarcoma found no difference between groups in overall or event-free 5 year survival. A meta-analysis reached a similar conclusion.

A meta-analysis identified 7 studies with 3433 patients comparing the MAP regimen (methotrexate + doxorubicin + cisplatinum) to an alternative, largely MAP + 1 or 2 additional agents. There was no statistically significant difference in 3 year or 5 year disease-free survival or overall survival.MAP chemotherapy had lower incidence of toxicities- including thrombocytopenia, febrile neutropenia, anemia, hypophosphatemia.
Mifamurtide is an option in combination with post-operative combination chemotherapy in patients with osteosarcoma, based on NICE clinical guidance.
Mirfamurtide + MAP chemotherapy for patients with localized osteosarcoma resulted in improved overall survival.
There is no evidence that calcitonin is effective for bone pain due to osteosarcoma.

The bisphosphonate zoledronic acid has been assessed in a systematic review as to efficacy in reducing progression and metastases but was found to be ineffective with both reduced overall survival and increased adverse events.
Wide margins, yet preserving limb function, is the goal of surgical therapy since narrow margins are associated with increased rate of recurrence.
There is evidence that the most useful predictors for local recurrence following surgery are margins of less than 2 mm and tumour necrosis rate of less than 90% following neo-adjuvant chemotherapy.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of pathological fracture on outcome has shown that it is not associated with increased risk of local recurrence but does predict for increased risk of subsequent metastasis and reduced overall survival.
Surgical resection of any metastases at any point in the course of the disease is critical to survival.

CT scan may underestimate the occurrence of multiple lung metastases and therefore open thoracotomy with palpation of all lung tissue and subsequent resection is recommended. Sixteen-channel multidetector row chest CT with thin sections was only 34% sensitive and has not been found to be useful to evaluate for pulmonary nodules in patients with osteosarcoma.
There is a 30% rate of reoperation and risk of infection(17.9%), death (7.3%), amputation (4.6%), and implant revision (4%) within the first post operative year
Physical therapy and rehabilitation are recommended to maintain limb function after surgical excision.

The most frequent symptom in patients with bone cancers and metastasis is pain. Calcitonin has been hypothesized to relieve pain symptoms in this population; however, the evidence has not been shown to support this.

Addition of pembrolizumab to preoperative radiotherapy and surgery improves disease-free survival for patients with stage III undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma and pleomorphic or dedifferentiated liposarcoma of the extremity
Five-year survival is approximately 60% with lower survival in patients older than 45 years of age, and improved survival in more recent years (65% vs 47%). B
A systematic review confirms that pathological fracture is a negative prognostic indicator with worse 5 year survival.
Death from osteosarcoma is usually by lung metastasis. C

After treatment, surveillance with history, physical examination, and radiographs of the chest and primary tumor site should occur every 3 months for the first 2 years, every 4 months for the third year, every 6 months for the following 2 years, and annually thereafter. B
Screening for pulmonary metastases can cease at 5 years in grade 1 tumours but should continue for up to 10 years for higher grades.
Course of untreated disease results in tumor progression and metastasis.
Death usually occurs because of pulmonary metastasis.
Five-year survival is approximately 60% with lower survival in patients older than 45 years of age, and improved survival in more recent years (65% vs 47%).
For patients with osteosarcoma near the knee undergoing limb-salvage surgery, a retrospective cohort study with mean 57 month follow-up found 62% 5 year survival and prosthesis survivorship in 77%.
Histologic response is the most important prognostic factor for osteosarcoma of the extremity.

Patients presenting with evidence of metastasis with initial diagnosis have worse 5year prognosis (8-35% depending on histology). Among patients initially without metastasis, development of metastasis, especially to lung and bone, is associated with a worse prognosis (24% vs 89% 5-year survival), as is development of local recurrence (36% vs 62% 5-year survival). Elevated lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase are also associated with worse outcomes.
Among patients with second, third, or fourth recurrences, 5-year survival is poor (12%-16%).
A large cohort study found that childhood survivors of bone cancer are at a high risk of at least 1 subsequent life-threatening or disabling event (64%).
There is a substantial increase in risk of second malignancy in survivors of young adult bone tumours.

Age >39years, the presence of distant metastasis, no history of having undergone any surgery, and tumor size >103mm are associated with poor prognosis (Peng) Primary tumors of the mandible and no history of having received radiotherapy are associated with a more favorable prognosis. Some evidence to suggest that the methylation of 7 genes DENND1B, EP400, MGC15885, TLN2, TTLL4, PTPRF, C3orf31 have prognostic capacity and may function as an underlying therapeutic targets.

M6A regulators are a proteins that stop RNA repair by regulating the activity of DNA repair proteins. Some evidence to show that aberrancy in the activity of the m6A regulators METTL3, YTHDC1, and FTO are prognostic of poor overall survival.

Surveillance following treatment should occur every 3 months for the first 2 years, every 4 months for the third year, every 6 months for the following 2 years, and annually thereafter. Visits should include history, physical examination, CXR, and radiographs of the primary tumor site.
Surveillance for local recurrence with X-ray should occur for at least 10 years. MRI should be performed if recurrence is suspected.

Lung metastasis can occur even after local treatment and chemotherapy. CT of the chest should be performed at 3 to 6 months postoperative, every 3 to 6 months for 5 years, and annually at least until year 10.
Less than 1% of patients with Paget's disease develop osteosarcoma.

Thirty percent of osteosarcomas occur in patients older than 40 years. When it occurs in adults, osteosarcoma usually occurs in patients with long-term, polyostotic disease and occurs in the 7th decade of life.
Treatment of osteosarcoma does not seem to differ between those with and without Paget's disease.
